opus-5.5.text:
I think the pace is actually faster than most people expected even a year or two ago, but it's also uneven, and I'd separate it into a few layers.

At the level of intent, almost every serious robotics company has now accepted that the future is model-based. Nobody really believes anymore that you can hand-engineer a pipeline for every task, every object, every environment. So the strategic shift has already happened. Companies are building data collection infrastructure, setting up teleoperation fleets, and training large policies or world models. That part has moved very quickly.

At the level of actual deployment, it's slower, and I think that's healthy. What we see is that models are first entering settings where the environment is semi-structured and the cost of failure is manageable: logistics, sorting, some factory tasks, warehouse picking. In those places, a model that works ninety-something percent of the time, with a human or a fallback system covering the rest, can already create value. But in open, unstructured homes, or in safety-critical settings, we're still far from that. The gap between a nice demo and something that runs for thousands of hours without intervention is very large, and closing it is mostly an engineering and data problem, not just a modeling problem.

The third layer, which I think people underestimate, is the data loop. In language models, the internet gave us the data for free. In robotics, every bit of data has a cost, and it's tied to specific hardware. So the companies that move fastest won't necessarily be the ones with the best architecture on paper. They'll be the ones that get robots deployed early, even in limited roles, and then use that deployment to collect real-world data and feed it back into the model. Deployment and model progress aren't sequential; they drive each other.

That's why I'm also quite interested in simulation and generative world models. If we can generate realistic, physically plausible interactions, we can lower the cost of data dramatically and speed up the whole cycle. It won't replace real data, but it can amplify it.

So my overall assessment: the direction is settled and the momentum is real, but the deployment curve will look gradual for a while. Then, once a few companies close the data flywheel in a meaningful domain, I think we could see a sudden acceleration, much like what happened with language models.

r002.rationale: It says robotics companies have accepted a model-based future and are moving beyond hand-engineered pipelines toward training large policies or world models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the pace is uneven, and that unevenness is the most interesting part of the story.

If you look at where the attention and the capital are going, it feels like everyone has already decided that robotics will go the way language and vision went: collect enough data, train a large model, and the robot will generalize. And in demos, that story looks almost finished. You see a dual-arm system folding a shirt, pouring water, picking things it has never seen before, and you think, this is close.

But deployment is a different question from capability. When I talk to companies actually putting robots into factories or warehouses, most of them are still running what I'd call hybrid systems. There is a learned component, maybe a vision model for grasping or a policy for one narrow skill, wrapped inside a lot of traditional engineering: hard-coded state machines, safety limits, calibration routines, and fallback logic. The "model" is doing one piece of the job, not the whole job. That is very different from the end-to-end picture in the demos.

So I'd separate it into three speeds. The research labs and well-funded startups are moving very fast on the model side, because the recipe is now fairly clear and the cost of trying things has dropped. Integrators and traditional robotics companies are moving carefully, because their customers care about uptime and recovery behavior, not about generality. And the actual deployed base, the robots doing real work every day, is moving slowest of all, because replacing something that works at ninety-nine point something percent reliability with something that works at ninety-five percent but is "smarter" is not an obvious trade.

There is also a data problem that I think people underestimate. In language, the internet gave us the data for free. In robotics, every piece of data costs money: someone has to teleoperate, or a robot has to run in the world and fail. So the companies that are moving fastest toward model-based deployment are often the ones who found a way to make data collection a byproduct of a real business, rather than a separate expense. That is a business design question as much as a technical one.

My overall read is that the direction is not in doubt anymore. Almost nobody is betting against learned policies becoming the core of the stack. But the timeline for broad, boring, profitable deployment is longer than the demo cycle suggests. I'd rather see companies be honest about which parts of their system are learned and which are engineered, because that honesty is actually what lets them move faster. The teams that pretend everything is already a model tend to get stuck when the first customer asks what happens at two in the morning when the robot does something strange.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts demos of individual robot tasks with factory deployment, where it says hybrid systems remain common. It does not describe a shift toward demonstrating that models work in factories.

r002.rationale: It says learned policies are expected to become the core of the stack, while deployed systems still wrap learned components in traditional engineering—clearly conveying movement toward model-based approaches.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between how quickly companies are experimenting and how quickly they’re deploying robots reliably. Experimentation is moving fast. Teams are increasingly willing to use learned models for perception, planning, and control. But getting a robot to perform a task in a demonstration is very different from having it do that task all day, with changing conditions and very little human intervention.

So I think the pace will be uneven. In structured environments, where the task is well defined and failures are manageable, deployment can move relatively quickly. For more general tasks, companies still have to solve reliability, data collection, and cost together. The real signal is how much useful work a robot can do between interventions—and whether that improves as the company gathers more experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the pace is uneven. Companies are moving quickly on demonstrations, but deployment moves at the speed of reliability. A robot can perform a task impressively once, and you still have a lot of work to do before it can repeat that task across different environments and recover when something goes wrong.

The companies that can deploy in a constrained setting, collect data, and use that data to improve the model have a practical path forward. So I would look less at how often a company releases a new model and more at how much useful work its robots are doing, how often people need to intervene, and whether those numbers are improving.

r001.rationale: It contrasts impressive one-off demonstrations with reliable deployment across environments, but does not identify a shift toward showing models working in factories.
